taxodist

Taxonomic hierarchy distances and lineage analysis in R, Python, and Julia

   

taxodist retrieves ordered taxonomic lineages from The Taxonomicon and compares hierarchy nodes through the depth of their most recent common ancestor (MRCA). The R, Python, and Julia packages implement the same distance definition and lineage semantics.

Usage guide · Web application · Function reference

What does taxodist measure?

For two ordered lineages, taxodist finds their continuous common prefix. The final node in that prefix is their MRCA. Distance is then defined as

\[ d(A,B)= \begin{cases} 0, & \text{if the complete lineages of } A \text{ and } B \text{ are identical}, \\ \dfrac{1}{\operatorname{depth}(\operatorname{MRCA}(A,B))}, & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

A deeper shared ancestor produces a smaller distance. Zero is reserved for identical hierarchy nodes; distinct nodes always have a positive distance, including when one taxon is an ancestor of the other.

Classification distance, not evolutionary distance

The values describe separation in a taxonomic classification. They are not evolutionary time, genetic distance, morphological divergence, or phylogenetic branch length. Dendrograms produced from the matrix summarize these classification distances and must not be interpreted as inferred phylogenetic trees.

Within each connected hierarchy, the definition is an ultrametric. Lineages with no shared root have infinite distance, while taxa whose lineages cannot be retrieved produce missing values in multi-taxon results.

Basic workflow

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
library(taxodist)

taxa <- c(
  "Tyrannosaurus",
  "Velociraptor",
  "Triceratops",
  "Homo sapiens"
)

# Retrieve an ordered lineage
lineage <- get_lineage("Tyrannosaurus")

# Compare two hierarchy nodes
result <- taxo_distance("Tyrannosaurus", "Velociraptor")
result$mrca
result$distance

# Build and analyze a community matrix
mat <- distance_matrix(taxa)
cluster <- taxo_cluster(mat)
ordination <- taxo_ordinate(mat)

plot(cluster)
plot(ordination)
import taxodist as td

taxa = [
    "Tyrannosaurus",
    "Velociraptor",
    "Triceratops",
    "Homo sapiens",
]

# Retrieve an ordered lineage
lineage = td.get_lineage("Tyrannosaurus")

# Compare two hierarchy nodes
result = td.taxo_distance("Tyrannosaurus", "Velociraptor")
result["mrca"]
result["distance"]

# Build and analyze a community matrix
matrix = td.distance_matrix(taxa)
cluster = td.taxo_cluster(matrix)
ordination = td.taxo_ordinate(matrix)
using Taxodist

taxa = [
    "Tyrannosaurus",
    "Velociraptor",
    "Triceratops",
    "Homo sapiens",
]

# Retrieve an ordered lineage
lineage = get_lineage("Tyrannosaurus")

# Compare two hierarchy nodes
result = taxo_distance("Tyrannosaurus", "Velociraptor")
result.mrca
result.distance

# Build and analyze a community matrix
matrix = distance_matrix(taxa)
cluster = taxo_cluster(matrix)
ordination = taxo_ordinate(matrix)

Core API

Task Functions
Retrieve and resolve taxa get_lineage(), get_lineage_by_id(), get_taxonomicon_id(), taxo_search()
Compare two lineages taxo_distance(), mrca(), shared_clades(), compare_lineages(), taxo_path()
Work with communities distance_matrix(), focal_distances(), closest_relative(), check_coverage()
Test clade membership is_member(), filter_clade()
Analyze and visualize taxo_cluster(), taxo_ordinate(), taxo_heatmap()
Manage retrieval caches cache_info(), save_cache(), load_cache(), clear_cache()
Load the offline reference object load_taxobase()

Reproducible reference data

R provides the taxobase data object, while Python and Julia provide load_taxobase(). Release 0.6.0 preserves the same component structure, taxon order, matrices, examples, and provenance metadata across the three implementations, using native containers in each language.

This object is useful for demonstrations, tests, and reproducible examples that should not depend on live network access. Live Taxonomicon queries may change as the underlying classification is updated.

Data source and citation

All retrieved lineage data originate from The Taxonomicon, based on Systema Naturae 2000. Published analyses should cite both the taxodist software and the underlying classification source:

Brands, S.J. (1989 onwards). Systema Naturae 2000. Amsterdam, The Netherlands. Retrieved from The Taxonomicon, http://taxonomicon.taxonomy.nl.
